rows: Acrylamide can form in some starchy foods during high-temperature cooking.
Food businesses should identify processes and products where acrylamide may form.
Mitigation measures should be proportionate to the business and food.
Raw-material selection can influence acrylamide formation.
Time and temperature controls can reduce formation.
Recipe and process changes may be appropriate where product quality and safety are maintained.
Monitoring and verification can demonstrate that mitigation measures are working.
Controls should be reviewed when ingredients, equipment or processes change.
Food colour or cooking time alone does not establish acrylamide concentration.
Conclusions require product, raw material, recipe, temperature, time, process, sampling and laboratory evidence.
Novel foods require authorisation before they are placed on the GB market.
The official GB register lists authorised novel foods and conditions of use.
Authorisations can specify compositional, labelling and population restrictions.
Businesses should confirm that the exact ingredient and intended use are covered.
Pre-EU-exit authorisations retained in UK law are included in the register.
New authorisations take effect through the current GB regulatory process.
Product identity and manufacturing process are important to applicability.
Changes to use level or target population may fall outside an existing authorisation.
A similar ingredient name or marketing claim does not prove authorisation.
Conclusions require exact identity, process, use, dose, population, conditions and register evidence.
Operators of septic tanks and small sewage treatment plants must meet applicable general binding rules.
Qualifying systems can operate without a permit only when all relevant rules are met.
A septic tank discharge to ground must use a suitable drainage field.
Septic-tank effluent must not be discharged directly to a watercourse.
Systems should be correctly designed, installed and maintained.
Planning permission and building-regulation approval may also be required.
If the rules cannot be met, connection to sewer, system change or a permit may be required.
A tank type or historic installation date does not prove compliance.
Conclusions require discharge route, volume, start date, system standard, maintenance, location, pollution and permit evidence.
Business oil-storage rules apply to specified oils and container capacities in England.
Containers should be strong, suitable and resistant to damage.
Storage location should minimise impact and collision risks.
Secondary containment is required for relevant storage arrangements.
Bunds and drip trays must have adequate capacity and integrity.
Remote filling arrangements should control delivery spills.
Pipework, valves and ancillary equipment should be protected and maintained.
Operators remain responsible for pollution caused by storage failures.
A tank capacity or inspection sticker does not prove full compliance.
Conclusions require oil type, capacity, location, container, bund, pipework, maintenance and spill-response evidence.
